utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearance for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you both. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman and I'm here with Milan Trbojevic. Ms. Jevtovic will be along, she's struggling with a copy machine to get some exhibits ready for you for today, we hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon to you both. Before we start -- I mean in the meantime, the usher can go and bring in the witness. I am trying, I've instructed Mr. Von hebel to see how possible it is to shift the afternoon sittings of the week 3rd to 7th February to the morning. I understand that Simic will not be sitting in the courtroom, although it willing doing something else, it will not be sitting in Courtroom III in the morning. So if it is at all possible, and if I have -- if we have your okay, we'll try and sit in the morning rather than in the afternoon. All right? 3rd to 7th. I will confirm it to you later, obviously, because I don't have a confirmation yet. But I've asked him to inquire about that and to arrange -- make the necessary arrangements with you, Madam Chuqing, as well. All right? So I will update you on that. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just trying to think what that does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is a problem we can always shift on any one of those days to the afternoon. Again, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour knows that I'm going to the U.S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'm flying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're still going? You're still adamant about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't have any choice. I'm flying back on the 5th of February which means I would arrive here on the morning of the 6th on. So if we switch to the mornings it means I will miss 4 of the sitting days that week instead of the three that I planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tell me what your preference is and I'm sure that Ms. Korner won't raise any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My preference is always to sit in the mornings, Your Honour, but I don't want to get the Prosecution into a witness bind because I know that they are trying to schedule crime base witnesses for those days that I'm gone, and I don't know whether he they can do four. I know they can probably pull off three.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can because the witnesses after that, we originally intended for the witness from the United Nations to testify that week, but because of Mr. Ackerman's problems he's been rescheduled. So all that week will be crime business witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That will work fine then. The other thing, Your Honour, is I've given you copies of these calendars today where I have put Xs in the days that I would like to have for intense preparation days so that they should be up there. They were handed to you by Chuqing; I saw her do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have this. This is what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How are we supposed to distinguish -- I have -- let's go through it. Page 1, I have the timetable for this month and I have two and three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ignore the numbers. That's just so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no markings on this first page, so I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have no comment. The second, February, it's -- I have 4, 5 and 1. Am I to ignore those numbers as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Those numbers are just used to counts the number of weeks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I have the week of the 17th to the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With four crosses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That we do not sit on those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And then March, there are no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: March, there are none. April you will see four more days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: April, we are talking of Easter which is on the 20th of April. And you're suggesting that we don't sit from Tuesday the 22nd to Friday, the 25th? When did you receive this, Ms. Korner? Today?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before Your Honours came in. Your Honours, all I can say is we repeat our request to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just have a look at it and discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've looked at it. I'm aware of what Mr. Ackerman is asking for, and my request remains the same and that is we sit all the days allocated on the Court calendar. Obviously, it's a matter for Your Honours having heard from Mr. Ackerman what you want to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to say very briefly that sitting continuously, I understand why the Prosecution wants to do that because it gives the Prosecution a very distinct advantage over us because they have a number of people to deal with things, we don't. I have a stack of documents this high that had been given me since the end of December, that I haven't even had a chance to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have Mr. Trbojevic on whom you can rely and Madam Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not at all. I have to look at the documents myself, Your Honour. Every one of them. If I didn't, I'd be delinquent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will discuss it among ourselves and we will come back to you. In the meantime, I prefer to go -- proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think I can allow that side crack to pass, just to say this: It's not that we look for the advantage. We are conscious because it's been raised so often of the length of time this trial is taking and the fact that the public expects us to sit the potential days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other hand, the public ought to know that I for one do consider that there is an obvious disparity of arms between the Prosecution and the Defence as far as resources are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought we had discussed this before. As Your Honour knows, it isn't that the lawyers who turn up from time to time in this case are just working on this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. But still the resources are different.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to argue with that but I don't want it to be thought, Your Honour and I thought we had mentioned this before, that each and every one of the lawyers who appears in this Court is solely working on this case. Each and every one of them is working on other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also want to thank you on behalf of everyone for your cooperation, which enabled another witness to return home where he was urgently needed. We do appreciate that very much. Before we proceed with your testimony, could I ask you to repeat your solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. And Mr. Ackerman will continue and hopefully finish -- hope, hope -- with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour on that line I'll try but it's unlikely and Ms. Korner knows that I will probably at least take the whole day. As you know, it's not totally up to me how fast this moves but I'll do the best I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel, and welcome back. And I hope you found a way to enjoy yesterday's respite from being in court.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to start again with your statement from the year 2000 and the Prosecution might as well give you all your statements so that we don't have to wait and we can work our way through them. I'm going to be referring in the next few moments to -- it's page 8 of the English version. It might very well be page 8 of your version too. There is a paragraph that begins, might be the easiest to find, "The Manjaca training ground was strictly a military training facility."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. If you just look down a couple of paragraphs, you'll see the one that I will be talking with you about. Now, after you retired from the army, you continued to live in Banja Luka until May of 1995, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During that time, you frequently contacted officers of the VRS and had conversations with them?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you said that the Bosniaks and Croats who saw you talking to these VRS officers thought you were a Serbophile and a real officers of the VRS, in fact, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is their opinion. I can't say as to what people think of me but it was to be expected for them to be suspicious of me and to have their doubts about me, but that is up to the individual in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how did you learn that the Bosniaks and Croats who saw you talking to the VRS officers had this suspicion? How did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone were to pass by me in the street without saying hello, then one has to stop and think why, whether there are any reasons, and probably the reasons were, as I was -- because I was with my colleague officers in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when was it that people were seeing these conversations and having these feelings about you being a Serbophile? Would that have been right after you retired?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had contact before retirement and after my retirement with them. I was of pro-Yugoslav orientation. I wanted a joint state, a joint army; however, people understood that differently, certain individuals. But that is up to them. They are entitled to do that. I didn't reproach them for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As long as you have mentioned that, I'd like to ask you a little bit about what you mean. Clearly, you were against -- being pro-Yugoslav, you were against the break-up of Yugoslavia at all, against the secession of Croatia and Slovenia at the very beginning, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a political issue. I was a professional soldier. I took my oath of allegiance to the Yugoslav People's Army. I grew up in a multi-ethnic environment, and it was normal to expect me to continue to uphold a common state. However, I was unable to bring any influence to bear on developments. I did my job as a professional, as a soldier, and not as a politician. But I was not indifferent to what was happening to all the peoples in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and especially to the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I felt that the policy that was being pursued in those days would not benefit any single nation in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I got an answer to the question. Let me try again. When you say that you were pro-Yugoslav, you're speaking of the Yugoslavia that existed before the independence of Croatia and Slovenia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was and to this day, for a community of all peoples. Therefore the people of Croatia and the people of Slovenia decide their destiny and I had no right to interfere. Just as the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina had decided at their own plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The after Croatia and Slovenia had become independent, would you say that you were still pro-Yugoslav? That you wanted to take what was left and keep Yugoslavia together in that form?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in favour of a common state, a confederal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you go over, sir, I think just one page, it's right -- the paragraph is, "In the middle of July, 1992." What you tell us there is that in the middle of July, 1992, you were elected to be the commander of the resistance staff in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes, page 9, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who was it that elected you to be the commander of the resistance staff in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A group of citizens of Bosniaks in Banja Luka was following and assessing the political security situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and particularly in Banja Luka and the Bosanska Krajina. In Banja Luka, there were a number of arrests of Bosniaks, instances of mistreatment. A certain number were even killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question was not what was going on in Banja Luka. The question was: Who was it that elected you to be the commander of the resistance staff in Banja Luka? It's a simple question. Who elected you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A group of citizens from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And were these citizens Bosniak, Croat, Serb? What was the ethnicity of the group that elected you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No Croats?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No Serbs?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did this group have any meetings?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did have meetings. We made assessments of the situation in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How large was this group?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were seven of us in the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you say about that group was the formation of the group, "This decision was taken to protect the non-Serb population who had nothing to do with the planned resistance." What decision was that? That was the decision not to do sabotage? Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was our judgement that the political security situation, and the attitude of the Crisis Staff and other bodies, was directed against the Bosnian people, Bosniak people in Banja Luka. And we feared that someone might, through acts of sabotage against units of the Army of Republika Srpska and their facilities, might provoke revolt on the part of the army and the police, or rather reaction on their part, and that a situation similar to the one that arose in Kozarac might develop, because religious buildings, mosques and other buildings, were destroyed in Banja Luka over a period of time of 15 days, and we considered this to be a provocation, to provoke armed resistance and to spark a massacre and complete ethnic cleansing of Banja Luka of Bosniaks. And for that reason, we prevented any acts of sabotage or diversions, even on the part of individuals, Bosniaks, and fortunately, this was complied with and there were no acts of sabotage. We did not provide a pretext to the authorities and the army in Banja Luka, even though, in those days, more than 250 Bosniaks were killed, individuals were found in the Vrbas River. There were large-scale arrests of men and women, mistreatment, people evicted from their homes, et cetera. So that people moved out of Banja Luka en masse, which we supported in those days because we feared that people might be physically liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've indicated that your mission was protection of the Bosnian -- of the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And is what you're telling us that one of the ways you went about that was to restrain the non-Serb population from engaging in provocative activities, basically?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to restrain the non-Serb population but to prevent the non-Serb population, because there were no activities of that kind; they were prevented. And this saved both the Croat and the Bosniak population in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These -- to be able to do that, of course, the word had to get out in the community that you didn't want any of these kind of things happening. You had to communicate that in some way to the non-Serb population, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I guess by the time you did that, that these people you were talking about earlier, these Bosniaks and Croats who thought you were a Serbophile, must have learned differently after you were commander of the resistance staff, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only a small number of people were aware of this resistance movement. Throughout my time in Banja Luka, people avoided me, were suspicious of me, and I wasn't angry about that because maybe that would have been my reaction too if I had been in their place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In effect, what you did at that point in time was you became a spy, an espionage agent of the Bosnian government, reporting what you could learn from the VRS; that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. You are insulting me. I was not a spy. I just decided to defend my people from genocide, which was being committed by the army, the para army and the official policies of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, even before you left the military, while you were still an active VRS officer, you were passing information through your son to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As an officer, I felt hurt, as a JNA officer, because on the 12th of March, 1992, I was appointed chief of a group for cooperation with the United Nations in Bosnian Krajina. And then on the 8th of March, 26 days later, I was replaced because I was considered politically unsuitable, and from that it became clear to me what was in the making, that I was unsuitable, and I didn't take an oath of allegiance to the Army of Republika Srpska. I was no spy, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're aware, because I know you've read it, that a gentleman named Muharem Krzic in his book says that while you were still active with the VRS, that you were passing information to him to be passed on to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina through your son. You complained to him that he had used the wrong name that it was a different son than he had mentioned in his book. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't provide Mr. Muharem Krzic information to pass on to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I gave him information about events in Banja Luka and the possible repercussions that the behaviour of the army and the police and the paramilitary could have for the Bosniak people, and what we needed to do to prevent genocide. And I did certainly want this to be conveyed to the government so that diplomatic or whatever measures needed should be taken so that Kozarac should not be repeated and other events that I don't need to mention. Yes, my son did take the information to Muharem Krzic, and I wanted to inform him as a prominent man from Banja Luka who passed on this -- to whom he passed on that information, I never asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In this courtroom, sir, on the 15th of January, page 12 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry Your Honour we are back on this little topic again. I object to what one witness has said being put to another. That's not a proper way of cross-examination. It's a comment. It can be drawn to Your Honour's attention in a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have had this happening already in the past, and we adopted the system that you don't tell the witness that some other witness has said this or that. You just suggest -- make -- put to the witness what you want to ask him and then, if necessary, confront him with the fact that this was stated by someone else but. First, you put to the witness your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm totally baffled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So am I, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How do you and Ms. Korner know what question I was going to ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were about to read out from a transcript of the sitting of the 5th --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 15th of January, that was last week, Your Honour, and Muharem Krzic wasn't here last week. She's not paying attention, that's all that's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see what --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it started this way, the question -- now I've lost it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said in this courtroom, sir, on the 15th of January --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I appreciate it could have been the 15th of January last year when Muharem Krzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The trial hadn't started yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Think before you -- I'm sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Before we go any further, can we establish this? If what Mr. Ackerman is about it do is put and tell this witness what another witness has said by saying, this is what another witness has said, that is inadmissible. What he of course, he can do is put a suggestion to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Simply saying, "Do you agree or disagree with it?" And not -- it is unnecessary and improper in my submission to state that this is what another witness has said and mention the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is completely ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear the question first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I had no intention of asking such a question, none at all. I specified January 15th. That had to be last week, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it had to be last week but let's hear what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, last week, on January 15th, you were asked by Ms. Korner about your exclusion from these one half hour -- exclusion by one half hour from these meetings that were going on with the corps commander. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said in your testimony that you were personally hurt by being excluded this half hour before where the others met together and you weren't there and that you presumed that they were discussing tasks of the corps within its area of responsibilities that they did not want you to hear. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was because you believed that they did not fully trust you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my assumption, because the meeting would begin at 7.00, I would be invited to come at half past 7.00, so I concluded from that that they were discussing reports which I, as a Bosniak, should not hear, and of course, this hurt me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in fact, they were right, weren't they? Because were you actually working as a spy, passing information to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I was not a spy. I simply stood up in defence of my people, to try and prevent the genocide committed in Kozarac and elsewhere. Not a spy but a Bosniak who was sorry that Yugoslavia broke up. It was broken up by those who threatened the Bosniaks, Croats, Macedonians and others, not a spy, sir, but a patriot. I can look the Serb people in the eye and each and every individual. It's not the Serb people that are to blame in my opinion but the leadership that led them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, once the war started, wasn't there a great deal of justification for the authorities being suspicious of non-Serb officers in the VRS and for dismissal of those officers?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they were dismissed, both Bosniaks and Croats and the Slovenes and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And by the 18th --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: By the 18th of May, that army was the army of the Serbian Republic and it had become a Serb army by May 18th, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Muharem Krzic whom we talked about, of course, was familiar with this resistance staff that you had been elected commander of, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any resistance movement that Mr. Muharem Krzic organised in Banja Luka. I hear this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, no. I'm talking about the one that you were the commander of. Muharem Krzic was aware of the existence of that organisation, of which you were the commander, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Muharem Krzic was not aware of this group of men. He just knew about me. And I didn't trust anyone, because I was afraid that due to naivete, people might damage the resistance movement staff in Banja Luka. I repeat, Mr. Muharem Krzic was not aware of the resistance movement in Banja Luka and its composition. He didn't even know that it existed, nor that I was the commander of that resistance movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After Muharem Krzic left Banja Luka, which was fairly early in 1992, you then had to establish a new contact. And who was that new contact that you began passing information to after Muharem Krzic left?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first associate in the resistance movement staff was engineer Sulejman Karabegovic and he was my closest associate, and I worked with him most of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But my question is: After Muharem Krzic, who you were passing information to through your son, left Banja Luka, you had to have some new contact to pass information to, and didn't you then begin passing information to Smail Djuzel?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I hear that for the first time and it's an allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another similar -- associated issue right now. In your testimony here on 17 January, you were asked the-- this following question and gave the following answer, Did you -- It's page 146 of the LiveNote -- I'm sorry, page 69 of the LiveNote, day 146. "Q. Did you take any physical action to investigate any arming of any resistance groups? In other words, did you yourself procure or supply any weapons to any group that was resisting the Serbs? "A. Not a single weapon. Not a single bullet. We did not plan any armed action, no sabotage. We did not have any weapons. We did not give any to anyone." Now, that's referring to this resistance group that you were the commander of, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it that remains your position today, that that resistance group, neither planned nor engaged in any kind of armed resistance or meant to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There weren't any weapons, nor was there any plan for armed action or sabotage by the staff of the resistance movement in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to take a look at Exhibit P282, please. Sir, this is a document dated 15 July, 1992, apparently signed by Colonel Zdravko Tolimir from the intelligence affairs department of the 1st Krajina Corps. It speaks of an interview with a gentleman named Dzemo Becirevic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He was being asked about an individual by the name of Jahic, either Muhidin or Muhadim. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muhidin Jahic was a quarter master working with me. I knew him, warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What is reported here is this: "Becirevic does not know if Jahic has been hired by Colonel Selak to work at the logistics base. He is, however, quite sure that Jahic is the main person in charge of the military organisation and the arming of Muslims in Banja Luka and that he has lists of all the armed Muslims, unit by unit. Some of the weapons collected by Jahic are in the old JNA social centre in Vrbanja." Now, this person you say was working for you during that time, was he, in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Muhidin Jahic, the quartermaster, was already retired at that time. He was a very honourable man. However, he was too docile, and he didn't have a great professional knowledge of weapons. He knew nothing about them at all, but this is the first time that I'm seeing this document, and it's the first time that I learn about this. But what it says here is not correct. Mr. Muhidin Jahic unfortunately was not capable of doing this, and quite certainly he knew nothing about it and didn't know how to do anything like this and couldn't have do so therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you if this part is correct: Did you bring him back to work for you at the logistics base as a civilian employee following his retirement? Was he working there as a civilian employee in the early months of 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Jahic, once he retired, I didn't need him, need his services any more after that. There was no need for me to bring him into the logistics base at all and I did not bring him so this is misinformation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is another paragraph in this document that is on a different subject but while we are here I want to ask you about it. If you look down, I don't know, it's maybe, four paragraphs below what we are talking about. It says this and some of it is not translated: "A certain Java Jengici [phoen] and Goran Banjac are the main criminals blackmailing Muslims in Banja Luka by offering them protection for 2.000 Deutschmarks. They also blue up the optician shop belonging to Rasim Cengic who refused to give them 2.000 Deutschmarks a second time." Do you know anything about those people and that incident that's described there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know nothing about this. I know nothing about the threats either or the blackmail, and the man who wrote this, I don't know of him either. So please believe me when I say that I didn't want to see anything like this happening and had I known about it I would have taken steps to prevent it. The optician's shop belonging to Mr. Cengic really was blown up. He had to leave. I don't know what date this was on, and who the perpetrators were, but quite certainly it was not a Bosniak because the -- a person who wrote this needed somebody. He needed a culprit. He needed something to justify the blowing up of the mosques and other facilities, houses and so on. And the expulsion of the Bosniak population from Banja Luka and the Croats too. So as for this document, this unfortunately seems to have been written by Colonel Tolimir which was not a correct thing to do, because as a professional man, as a professional military man, he should never have written anything like this because quite simply, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like you to look at another document. It's DB121. Sir, this document was written by you, was it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it says that it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have the document on the ELMO, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, do have a copy of it, because it was actually originally included in our list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says that it was written for the attention of Mr. H. Osmanagic. Can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He worked in the embassy in Zagreb, the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia, in Zagreb, and this was written in 1995, I think in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was after you had left Banja Luka, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think out of an abundance of caution I would ask to go to private session just for the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. If you go a little ways down in the document under paragraph 2 -- let me ask you. There is a person mentioned in this document --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a person mentioned in this document just by the name Siber. Who is Siber?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Stjepan Siber was an officer of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Good friend of mine, since before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, it appears that what you did was send this with your son to your -- I think it's your brother Emir Selak, with instructions that he should deliver it to Mr. Osmanagic. Is that the way this was delivered?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the way it was delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look now under paragraph 2. The second paragraph under number 2 begins with, "In 1991, I refused to carry out the order of General Uzelac for arming the Serbs from Sipovo and Mrkonjic Grad because they wanted to go to Kupres to assist the JNA units that were fighting the Croats." Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. However, because of a lack of space here, I failed to write that General Uzelac asked that the -- not the formations where the mobilisation had taken place be armed. In this case, General Tolimir was informed, the assistant commander for logistics of the 1st military district in Belgrade. I informed him about this too. As proof and evidence, I can quote from my official notebook, which I have here, and I can find it in the notebook where it was recorded with the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's really not necessary. The point I'm trying to make here is that you knew at the time that there was a -- hostilities, fighting, going on between JNA units and Croatian units at Kupres, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you knew that by keeping men who wanted to go there to assist the JNA from being armed so they could do so, you might assist the Croatian fighters, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Quite the reverse. I insisted upon the fact that through legal, official military formations, with the right to bear weapons, be issued weapons, and the arming of the people would lead to in quite the opposite direction, sir, and actually, because of all this, I asked for the replacement -- I asked General Tolimir -- for a replacement. He refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go now to the next page. There is a paragraph that begins, "In November, 1991." What you say there is this: "In November, 1991"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I haven't found that portion. September you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, November. November 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Requested by the 5K, I assume that's the 5th Corps, to do --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- a survey of the machines at the factory of the fittings in Hrvatska Dubica and to check the possibility of quick dismantlement of the machines. I sent an expert team with a captain graduate machine engineer, my reliable man, who had stated in his report that the factory was intact and fully operational. I did not allow the machines to be dismantled, and because of that, the command of the 5th Corps and the political leaders of the SDS caused me a lot of problems, threatened me and so on." Now, the first question I want to ask you about that is what kind of machines are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Hvratska Dubica, there was a factory of armature -- reinforcement. When the units of the 5th Corps took control of Hrvatska Dubica, they informed General -- or rather the corps commander of the existence of this factory, whose machines ought to be dismantled, and sent to Serbia. Colonel Vukelic came to see me. He was the assistant of the corps commander for morale, and he asked me to carry out this task. I sent a professional team to Hrvatska Dubica and two days later, as the captain who was a mechanical engineer himself informed me, that the factory had remained intact and complete, and that all it needed was some inventory and material for reproduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was, try please to answer the question and nothing but the question. The question was: "Now, the first question I want to ask you about is: What kind of machines are we talking about here?" You should have just said -- answered what kind of machines you were referring to in your statement. And that was what was asked of you. Instead you went on to tell us a whole story, not that we -- I personally mind, but other -- if we continue like this, you're going to be here the rest of the week plus possibly also next week.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to say that this is a very essential question for me too, so I seek your indulgence. When I refused to dismantle the factory I had problems in the corps command and threats as well, and that's what I wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was coming later. But I have -- you have to answer the questions that are put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And try to restrict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's see, Colonel, if we can be a little more specific. These machines, what exactly is it that those machines did? What were they designed to do? What were they used for? What was built there? What was constructed there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a factory of fittings or armature for civil engineering, for construction work and projects, and I don't know who needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Pipe fittings or things like -- or what?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it. What I understood from the report was that it was construction material.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For civil engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But as I didn't see the factory myself, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, a few moments ago - and it's been longer than I expected it to be - we were talking about your testimony on page 69 of the LiveNote, and I want to go back to. I had asked you about your testimony regarding this resistance group that you commanded there in Banja Luka, and you had assured me that there -- it never did plan or have the weapons to put up any kind of armed resistance. And having told me that, and let me refer you then to that paragraph that begins, "In July 1992." And what you're saying there in this document that you wrote yourself for transmission to the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb was that, "A command post which I commanded was set up to offer armed resistance, armed resistance, to the Serbian troops in the region of Banja Luka. I will discuss this in detail when I see you."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea was along those lines, yes. But when we saw how great the military power was in Banja Luka, the Serbian Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina there and other armed formations, we assessed, we weighed up the situation and thought that this was quite crazy, if I can use the term, and that it would mean the annihilation of the Bosnian people. So we didn't do anything along those lines. We decided that we would take no armed action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there were no attempts to do so either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you were in that army. You handled the logistics for that army. When you planned to offer armed resistance, you knew what that army was, and that's not something you discovered later and caused you to change your mind, is it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, we weighed up the situation and decided what to do to protect our own people, how to protect it, and it was on the basis of this evaluation that we made the decision not to engage in to armed action and to prevent any sabotage, not to give cause for liquidation and the perpetration of genocide against the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Then you came into this Court and you told these judges, "We did not plan any armed action," and you confirmed that twice today, having been asked about it. And now you say, "Well we did plan armed action but we changed our minds."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- or rather no. We didn't plan it. We weighed up the pros and cons and the repercussions that this resistance would give rise to throughout the population. There was no plan of armed resistance, sir. Mr. Ackerman, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I need to you consult your notebook. I assume you have it with you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: January 1 of 1992, page 17 of the English version --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Under the heading, "Tasks of the 5th Corps Commander," as I understand -- if I remember your testimony the other day well, you said that these were tasks that the 5th corps commander was delivering to all of you, having gotten them through the federal secretariat for national defence. Is my memory right about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of those in January 1 of 1992 was to protect the Serbs in Republika Hrvatska from genocide. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we went through this the other day, so I'm going to skip over some material here. We will come back to your notebook a little later, sir. In your testimony -- see if I can find it -- it's your statement of 2001 to the Prosecutor, and I'd also like you to have document P15. The statement to the Prosecutor, on page 3, you speak of eight documents that you had brought with you. Can you find that part?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You say, "I have brought with me eight document that I would like to submit as evidence. I recently received these documents from the state security in Sanski Most. I cannot disclose the name of the person who gave me these documents." Now look, would you please, at P15? And that document, sir, is one of the documents you're speaking of that you brought from state security in Sanski Most and delivered to the Prosecutor, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your statement, it would be what's referred to as the fifth document, dated 24 August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, 24 August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the document, yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you were referring to the time when I received it. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in that statement, you say, and this was a statement made in, I think it was March of 2001, I'm not certain about that but it was made sometime in 2001, you say that you recently received them from state security in Sanski Most. How recently? How long before you gave your statement to the OTP had you been handed these documents?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the document itself, it says the 10th of March, 2001, and there is my signature attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So would that be the date you turned them over to the OTP or the date you received them from state security of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the date when I received the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that would be 10 March, 2001?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did you receive them in Sanski Most or were they brought to you by someone?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that is important. I received them on the 10th of March, 2001, and for reasons of security of that person, I do not wish to give the name of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think it's important. Did you go to Sanski Most to receive them? Were you there meeting with state security in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the document in Sanski Most. Those are documents which clearly indicate the intentions of paramilitary units, the intention to form them and use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You're answering a question you weren't asked. So you signed those documents indicating that you had received them from state security on 10 March, 2001, and then you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on that same date, 10 March, 2001?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can't be right. There must be a mistake. There was a time interval in between. I cannot remember the date. Then probably this is the date when I gave this document to the investigators. I would like to correct my statement. You are right. The date, the 10th of March, is the date when I gave this document to the investigators, because I asked to have a copy for myself, and I signed it for reasons of security. So that it should be known that it was my document and that I had handed it over. So I received it earlier, but I received it in 1991 [as interpreted]. I don't know exact date. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, out of an abundance of caution, can we go to private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, sometime in 2001, before March 10th, people with state security in Sanski Most were aware that you were going to be giving an additional statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, and with that knowledge, gave you documents to assist you and to assist the Prosecutor regarding that statement, did they not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I did not mention at all to the person who gave me this that I would be having any contact with the Prosecution. The man gave it to me because he trusted me and for me to have these documents for myself. In fact, I abused his trust. But in the interest of truth and evidence as to what was being planned and organised, I gave this to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your statement, I think, at the -- at the very end of that 2001 statement, the last paragraph, you said, "I will talk to the person who gave me these documents to inform him that he needs to inform the ICTY on how he obtained the above documents." Right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if that ever happened?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When was the last time you talked to the person who gave you these documents?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, and I don't remember ever meeting him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Over the last year, have you been following this case? Have you been watching the television regarding this case, or listening to it in any way? Have you been following this case?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not been following, and I'm not familiar with the details. I did see in daily news bulletins on television, certain reports when they appeared, but I am living in an area close to Sarajevo where there is no TV broadcasts because the antennas, the aerials are very poor. And I very rarely receive such information with the exception of what appears in the press so this can easily be checked. The settlement [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you spoken to anyone who has been a witness here about the testimony they gave while they were here? A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before that's answered I think we are in open session at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder whether that last full answer he gave which gives his exact address could be redacted, please, before it goes out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it give the exact address?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, to all intents and purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. That's being granted as requested, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The witness just said something. What did the witness say?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, that's what he said, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you spoken to anyone who has testified here in this case about their testimony here?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who has testified in this case. All the people who have testified. Certainly, a topic of discussion that cannot be avoided when talking to my friends is the Tribunal, the responsibility of individuals for what happened so that I don't know who has testified, nor did people tell me or confide in me, so I may have but I don't know that that person has testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was not specific enough with my question, sir, and let me try to do a better job. What I'm interested in is have you spoken with anyone who said to you, "I testified in the Brdjanin-Talic trial at The Hague and let me tell you about that?" Did you ever have a conversation like that with anyone who you know told you they testified here?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Adil Medic told me that he had come here and that he had testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about Adil Draganovic? Did you ever speak with him?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adil Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulty about this question is some people have testified openly. The witness may be allowed to name people who haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't remember if the last name mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Medic testified openly there is no question. I don't know who else the Colonel is going to go on and name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't object to going into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to private session and in the meantime, the last name mentioned by Mr. Ackerman will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 15 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, there is some confusion that I need to get cleared up. You'll remember at sort of the beginning of your session today, I showed you a document, it was P282, from the intelligence affairs department of the 1st Krajina Corps and it's signed by Colonel Zdravko Tolimir. There were a couple of names that I asked you. Let me just do this. Is it true that you do not know who Dzemo Becirevic is?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true, I do not know who Becirevic, whatever the first name is is. I never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other -- Zdravko Tolimir, you have heard of him or you knew who he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zdravko Tolimir was a Colonel. I don't know what position he held, I've forgotten, but I do know him -- I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's all. I want to go back now to that document, P15, that we were looking at. I think you may still have it there. If not, we will get it for you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the first part of this, there is a two-page part, which is basically a letter and this letter is signed by a person named Colonel Ostoja Dejanovic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you told us you have no idea who this person is, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I believe he came from the areas of Slovenia and Croatia and I really don't know Mr. Dejanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He calls himself, does he not, the commander?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, commander of volunteer units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Other than this document that we are looking at right here, it's the case, isn't it, that you never heard of a position of commander of volunteer units other than having read it on this document?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the units or the deployment of those units or their organisational structure. I had no access to that. Clearly the reasons are quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there were never any weapons requests, weapons distribution requests, like the ones we saw from the various TOs that came from the commander or any other officer of this -- these volunteer units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no requests, nor would I have approved them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you don't have any idea, do you, whether this letter was ever actually sent to anyone or not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I see this document for the first time, but it was addressed to municipal staffs of volunteer units in Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before you saw this letter, you never heard of something called municipal staffs of volunteer units, did you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't. I knew that volunteer units existed, but that there were municipal staffs, I hadn't heard of that, nor did I have any access to such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you made frequent visits to various municipalities. That was part of your job, to discuss matters occurring within those municipalities and you never heard that there was a municipal staff of volunteer units in any of those municipalities, did you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I visited only three municipalities in my area of responsibility, where my units are, for which I provided logistics, Mrkonjic Grad, Jajce, and Donji Vakuf, and Banja Luka, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And additionally, you cannot tell us, you do not know, if this document that is attached to this letter, if we can call it that, is actually the document that the letter refers to or some other similar document? You can't even tell us that, can you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, which I provided, is from the staff of volunteer units of Bosnian Krajina. I see this first document for the first time. I haven't read it, not now even.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the second document, you don't know, do you, that -- I'm sorry, you just said that you've seen it now for the first time. This is the document that was given to you by somebody at the state security service for your own personal collection. What do you mean you're only seeing it now for the first time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't understand one another, Mr. Ackerman. I am saying that I see for the first time the document signed by Colonel Ostoja Dejanovic. That's the one I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we just had a very long discussion before the break about you acquiring this document from someone whose name you don't remember with the state security service, and I asked you if it was acquired for the purpose both in your mind and that of that person, of bringing it to the Tribunal. And you said no, it was given to me for my own personal collection of documents. And now you're telling us you're seeing it for the first time. I don't understand. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a misunderstanding, Mr. Ackerman. I said that I have this document in my hands for the first time, the one signed by Colonel Dejanovic. This is the document that I'm seeing for the first time, and not this other one, which says, "Aims and principles of organising volunteer units in the territory of Bosnian Krajina," which I received for my personal collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ah, so it's only the second part, these last four pages, that were actually given to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the document given to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you recall, when I introduced this document into evidence, it was -- I'd originally put it as an attachment and I realised that a fuller version which was a letter plus the attachment had already been exhibited through Mr. Donia, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a matter of dispute whether that's a fuller version or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, Ms. Korner is right, because she did bring this out. Secondly, Mr. Ackerman, if you refer to the witness's statement itself, on the fourth page, top of the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm satisfied that he's correct that he only got this second part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The fifth document consists of four pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you really have no idea whether this letter and this document were originally together or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you'll agree with me that one of the possibilities is that both of these documents, that may or may not be related to each other, one of the possibilities is that they were draft documents that were never distributed to anyone. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Those documents did arrive in the institutions to which they were addressed, the municipal staffs and the combat [as interpreted] units, and they were addressed to them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, volunteer units not combat units.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So they did arrive at the institutions they were addressed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I guess we are just going to have to start all over. We just went through this whole process of you telling us you had never heard of a commander of volunteer staffs, you'd never heard of municipal staffs of volunteer units, that all you know about it is from looking at these documents, that you went to several municipalities, while were you in those municipalities you never heard of the municipal staff of volunteer units. And now all of a sudden, you're telling us that you know these documents was delivered to the municipal staff of volunteer units that you don't even know exist. How could that be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, just to make things clear, his answer was: "These documents did arrive in the institutions to which they were addressed, the municipal staffs, and the combat units." You're telling him or suggesting to him that he said that they went to the several municipalities and also to the municipal staff of volunteer units. He did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He said to the municipal staffs to which they are addressed. That's what it's addressed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It does. He said to municipal staffs of volunteer units. He said it went to municipal staffs to which it was addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which document to municipal staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one I have which is attached to his statement, it just says, the objectives and principles of organising volunteer units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're not looking at the cover letter, the alleged cover letter, signed by Colonel Dejanovic. It says that it's addressed to municipal staffs of volunteer units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the cover letter. I'm only talking of -- he is talking of the document that he saw at the time and that he knows about. He can't be testifying on the other document which he is seeing for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, just tell us how you know that this document, the four-page document that was given to you, was delivered to volunteer units.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was sent to and addressed to the volunteer units, there is no reason why they shouldn't have been delivered there --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where does it say?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where does it say it was addressed to them? Show us. Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say anywhere, but other documents also indicate that there was normal correspondence between the staffs, the municipal staffs, daily communications, in fact, so this document points us in that direction too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you told us you didn't know that there were such things as municipal staffs of volunteer units. You told us that. And then you told us that. And then you told us that this must have gotten there because it was sent there, but there is nothing on here indicating it was sent there. Why are you just making things up here? Why don't you give us a honest answer? You don't know that these were ever distributed anywhere, do you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I do know that the paramilitary formations, that's what I call them, were under the control of the crisis staffs, the municipal and regional ones, so this was normal correspondence between the two parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You don't know that this document was ever delivered to anybody, do you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't testify to that because I wasn't there. The document wasn't accessible to me. If that's what you're asking me, then my answer is I don't know. But from this document, it would emerge, it appears, we see, to whom it was sent and why it was sent, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's why I asked you about five times and you told these judges that you knew that it had been distributed to these people. Now you're saying, okay, you're right, you didn't know that? And the truth is you didn't know that. And you don't know it as you sit here today. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, it doesn't state in the document to whom it was sent. But it says the staff command of the volunteer units. So it's not written for one's own needs but for the needs of the subordinate units and organs. That's what I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you sat here and told these judges that you knew it had been delivered to the persons to whom it was addressed and the fact is it's not addressed to anyone, is it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that I knew that the document was addressed or not addressed. The document exists as such and as a professional soldier, I would expect that if a joint command existed, that they would all issue orders to me and inform me what my tasks and duties were. So I didn't say that I knew and was aware of these documents. I received them in the year 2001. That's when I saw them for the first time. So how should I know that they had existed before that and that the units had received this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's clear enough. I think we can move to something different, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, as a professional soldier, as a highly trained and skilled professional soldier, as someone who knows about documents and the regularity and irregularity of documents, look at this document, tell the judges what it is about this document that they should conclude would persuade them it's not a forgery. Tell me one thing -- tell us one thing about that document that you can use to conclude that it's genuine at all.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the title of the document itself, Mr. Ackerman, because it says, "The aims and principles of the organisation of volunteer units in the area of Bosanska Krajina." And the signature is the staff command of the volunteer units of Bosanska Krajina, and they are sending out information as to the ways and principles of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does yours have a signature?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does yours have a stamp?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you make a document authentic just by giving it a classy title?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that really is an argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Because the very first part of his answer was, look, it has a title. So he's attributing importance to the fact that a document has a title. So let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Rephrasing of the question would be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it. Colonel, the whole point that is being put to you - and I think in a very fair well as well by Mr. Ackerman - is this: Just as much as these documents were handed to you by a person, the identity of whom you don't want to reveal, in 2000 or in the year 2001, isn't it equally possible that these -- this document that was handed to you in 2001 is not an authentic document at all but it is a document that has been made up and handed over to you in the hope that this document would be made use of by you, little knowing that it is not an authentic document? This is what is being suggested to you by Mr. Ackerman, who has every right to interfere and intervene if he thinks that I have misinterpreted his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You haven't, Your Honour. That's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is not signed. That is true. There is no stamp either. And this brings us to a dilemma as to whether it is authentic or not, but I personally don't doubt it. That is my personal opinion. I do not doubt its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's another point. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let's look at another document, I'd like you to look at P229. Now, I take it, sir, that you know absolutely nothing about this document?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know by looking at it that it has no signature?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No signature but it does have a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the stamp?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a similar stamp, this is the Serbian Democratic Party, the Sanski Most board -- I think it's Sanski Most. I haven't seen this particular stamp, but I have seen similar stamps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It speaks about, if you look at the -- just the first paragraph, right under the word, "Conclusions," a subregional meeting of the representatives of several municipalities, Bihac, Bosanski Petrovac, Srpska Krupa, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Kljuc, does it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know if there ever was such a meeting of those municipalities, of your own personal knowledge, do you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, I did not have any personal knowledge. But after the war, I heard from others, from people, that this was what happened, but not during the war, I didn't then, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That this specific meeting happened? You say you heard about this specific meeting?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You don't know whether this document was ever actually sent to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Autonomous Region of Krajina or the 1st Krajina Corps, do you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You never saw it as an official document that arrived at the 1st Krajina Corps, did you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 7, it says in paragraph 7 that "This group proposes that Dr. Nikola Erceg finally form a government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." To your knowledge, Nikola Erceg never formed a government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, did he?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something was formed. Mr. Nikola Erceg was held high posts. Whether he was the Prime Minister or whatever, the Prime Minister of the government of the autonomous region I can't say. Many years have passed since then so don't held me to my word because I don't want to say anything that I'm not certain of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me be a little more specific because I didn't lead up to that properly. If you look at paragraph 6, you see that they are being very critical of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.
