And they say, "If the leadership of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in Banja Luka fails to solve this issue, our seven municipalities will take all Muslims and Croats under military escort from our municipalities to the centre of Banja Luka." So it's speaking about the existence of an Autonomous Region of Krajina and their dissatisfaction with the way it's operating, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the things that they are suggesting that might relieve their dissatisfaction is if they could get Dr. Nikola Erceg to form a government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, that would truly take care of the economy and evenly distribute the economic resources and potential of the municipalities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's all I have with that document. Thank you. I want to go to another issue now. In your testimony in the Tadic case, it's on page 1.246 of your testimony, the 5th of June, you were asked about paramilitary groups during that testimony, and specifically you were asked this question: "Q. Colonel Selak I would like to now ask you some questions about paramilitary activity. In your position in the JNA, did you become aware of any paramilitary units operating within your area in either 1991 or 1992?" And the answer you gave was this: You mentioned two groups in your answer. You said: "Yes, we called them red berets because they were wearing red berets on their heads. They were officially called Serb defence forces. The command was in the hotel Bosna in Banja Luka." Then you go on to discuss a second paramilitary formation that you were aware of that it was in Banja Luka at the time, that formation of a Miljanovic from Prnjavor, and you say "they were called the eagles or something like that," and that you had seen them near Prnjavor at one time at least. So you named two groups and one of them who you thought to be the Miljanovic group whom you thought to be the eagles. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Miljanovic's unit was at Prnjavor and I was coming back from Belgrade from my -- from a business trip. I was passing by and the traffic was being controlled by these people with knifes, tucked into their belts, hand grenades, and so on. They were bearing both civilian clothing and camouflage uniforms but they looked very, very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And those were the two paramilitary units that you were familiar with on 5 June, 1996, that were operating in your area in 1991 or 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And even though you thought they were called the eagles, you now know, I think that they were called the Wolves of Vucjak? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, you've brought me to a dilemma now. I don't know they were the White Eagles and the Wolves of Vucjak, and I can't really say now because I wasn't -- I stopped at Prnjavor. I wasn't there. I did see a paramilitary unit and I thought they were the White Eagles. Now whether they were the White Eagles, the Beli Orlovi, or not or whether they were the Wolves of Vucjak, I'm at not quite sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, whatever they were, they were a formation under the command of Milanovic from Prnjavor. That's you're certain of, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that particular unit, in the settlement of Lisnja had perpetrated a massacre in 1992 against the Bosniak people and set fire to nine houses, with Colonel Tepsic I intervened to calm the situation down and it was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir, I'm now going to be asked that you be given the 1st Krajina Corps war diary, and I have a couple of questions I want to ask you from that right now, and there will be more later. I want to you find the entry for -- you looked at it earlier -- 1 July, 1992. It's the first entry of that date.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What it says there, does it not, that at 1500 hours, Brdjanin came with his escort to visit the OG.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, the 1st of July, 1992, I have here, it says General Mladic, General Pliptic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 35, Your Honour, in the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I have the English one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, it could be very confusing because some of the pages from June actually say July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said first entry on that day, 1st July. If you look at the previous one, it's 30th July. At least that's the one that we have, page 28, the entry seems to be 30th July when it probably should be 30th of June. In any case, he needs to refer to ERN number 01304535.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right. The last few days of June in the diary are called July for some unexplainable reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's useless telling him to refer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've found it. Brdjanin came at 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With his escort to visit the OG, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: OG stands for what, operations group, operative group?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operative group, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would it be correct that that is a collection of units larger than a tactical group but formed basically for the same purpose?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a bigger one, of brigade composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bigger than a tactical group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. The entry doesn't say anything about who Brdjanin was or any position that he held, does it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you of course have no idea what Brdjanin did when he went there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was doing there but we know the aim of his arrival. That's quite clear, and I said that last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you don't know what he did when he went there. That's my question. You don't know what he did, do you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know if he met with General Talic, do you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know if he had any discussions with anyone regarding the situation at the front and the problems encountered by the army. Of your own knowledge, you don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but from the diary, as it's the same date, it says, "General Talic had talks and so on." Now, what we discussed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know if he made any assurances about what the government could or would do, do you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, but he did inform the command of the operations group, that is my assumption, as an officer. When a political person comes to me from the authorities, he brings information about the goals and how to realise them, put them into practice, and with his authority, he lent his support to the operations group units and its command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You just told us that from the diary on the same date it says, "General Talic had talks and so on." Where is that? Where did you find that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the first words, "General Talic had talks with the commanders," et cetera on the 1st of July. The page is 534, "General Talic talked to the commanders about the previous night," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that would have been in the morning of that day?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Brdjanin didn't arrive until 1500 hours, so that couldn't be related at all, could it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came at 1500 hours, yes, and what happened in the meantime, it doesn't state in the diary. So therefore I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know if Brdjanin saw or was seen by any of the rank and file troops who were actually doing the fighting, do you? Of your own knowledge, you don't know that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but from the diary, if he appeared in the operations group, then he must have known what was going on and he was informed by the commander of the operations group about the situation in the area of responsibility of the operations group. And so there was feedback, two-way information. That's what emerges from this. They informed each other. And that is standard military practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is one sentence, "At 1500 hours, Brdjanin came with his escort to visit the OG." Where does it say there that he met with the commander of the OG, and there was feedback and conversation between them. It's not there. You're just making that up, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's be fair with the witness. Isn't it normal in military practice that if someone is visiting the OG, he doesn't just walk in. There is a protocol that is followed. And if he's an important person like your client was at the time, he would be met by the commander and not by --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But if he was an unimportant person --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Person at the time and I will show you that in just a moment then he wouldn't be met by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, may I be allowed to state the following? In that case, the commander of the operations group wouldn't receiver him, nor could he come to the operations group. Some civilian with no authority or no power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're going to find out a little more about that in just a second. In your testimony here in this courtroom. Day 146, I think that was Thursday but I'm not certain, page 59, LiveNote, you were asked with this visit by Brdjanin at 1500 hours. And then you were asked, "Would you expects a visit from the person who was in charge of the government of the region to a military post?" And your answer was as follows, sir, the question is clear: "The units in the front visits by representatives of the government, the political organs, the general staff, these visits were something that were necessary. The people liked that. They liked to get information." Now listen clearly, "And from this diary, you can see clearly that the soldiers were satisfied. They were very happy with Mr. Brdjanin's visits to the units in the front. This meant moral support to them." That's what you told us. "From this diary, you can see clearly that they were satisfied and very happy." That's what you said. Right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I would be satisfied if I was the commander of a unit, if I were to receive a visit from a person age of that kind. It would be my pleasure and privilege to have been visited by somebody like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is not my question. My question is: You said that you can see clearly from the diary that the soldiers were satisfied that they were very happy with Mr. Brdjanin's visit, and you were referring to that sentence that says, "The soldiers were delighted and their morale rose significantly." That's what you think shows how they felt about Brdjanin's visit, right? And that's what you told us.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Between the sentence that talks about his visit and that sentence, there is a pretty important sentence, isn't there in it says, "At 1530 hours word came that Plehan and Rabic had fallen." Don't you think that would delight the soldiers and improve the morale a great deal more than seeing Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you're talking about and if you look next, "The Ustasha stronghold, a bastion of Catholicism and fascism, and a seed of hatred towards the Serbian people has fallen." Big deal. Much bigger than Brdjanin's visit. Okay?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both, sir, announcements, that is the arrival of Mr. Brdjanin and the capture of Plehan by the operative group were certainly well received by both officers and soldiers of the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also suppose they were happy to have received cigarettes at 1200 hours. That must have made them delighted and boosted their morale as well, Mr. Ackerman and Colonel Selak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it that someone of the -- of what you say was the stature and importance of Mr. Brdjanin was certainly free to come and visit various military units whenever he felt it was necessary for him to do so. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He wouldn't have had to get any kind of advanced permission from the commander to come into that area, would he? Like a pass to get through checkpoints or anything?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Visits of this level, Mr. Brdjanin and his associates needed to inform the command of the corps or the corps command that they were going to visit a subordinate unit or a tactical or an operative group or even a brigade, and in that event, somebody from the command would go with them but not necessarily, but the commander or the corps command needed to be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But they certainly didn't have to get any kind of special travel passes to allow them to pass through checkpoints or things like that because of their high government stature, people like Brdjanin, Karadzic, people like that. Right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they always had an escort. One would expect that they had personal bodyguards, checkpoints were aware of this, these were military and police checkpoints. Therefore it was normal for them to go to the staff commands of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at DB122, sir. What you have before you, sir, is a permit issued by General Talic that gives Mr. Brdjanin permission to travel along a certain route, Doboj, Prnjavor, Banja Luka, and his delegation, with nine people in four motor vehicles, that the permit cannot be used for other purposes. In other words, that he can't use it to travel anywhere else but just along that route, and that was issued 26 June, 1992, was it not? Just a few days before this visit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just said that the information had to reach the command. I didn't say whether it had to be in writing or orally, but the corps command had to be informed. I didn't know that they issued written documents for passage but the information had to be passed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also told us that a person of high stature, high government official, wouldn't need such a pass or a permit, and I suggest to you you're correct, but Mr. Brdjanin did have to get such a pass or a permit, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, Judge Janu is drawing my attention to a very important point here. The permits, permission is not being granted to Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. It states delegation has another nine people with four motor vehicles. So happens that the delegation is being headed by Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. So to say that this is a permission that is being issued to Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin because even a person like Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin required permission, probably he did, and I would expect that the permission would have had to be issued in any case, in a combat zone, where there were army posts, but army checkpoints. But please do take this into consideration, that the permit covers not just Mr. Brdjanin but a delegation which he was heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. The document itself says that it was he and his delegation that arrived there. And that's what I was talking about throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The document says he and his escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's different. The diary says at 1500 hours Brdjanin came with his escort, one, singular, to visit the operations group. While here we have delegation from the republic, Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, judge, I think it will become clearer to you as we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I would imagine -- I would expect everyone to need a permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know that's your position, and we'll see if you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Knowing something about army procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at, sir, at DB123 now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, there is a kind of an issue with regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, just for your assistant to take care of this, because I notice that the documents that you handed to us today begin with DB127, which presumes that we made use of DB126. In actual fact, DB126 yesterday was presented as DB126 initially but corrected because it was DB80 already filed on the previous occasion. So we don't have a DB126. So take care of that so that we don't have this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll get it all worked out. This one was DB123. What I wanted to tell Your Honours is this: When this was all initially prepared I expected to use only one page from this logbook. And then as time went by, I realised I needed to use some additional pages, so I submitted another exhibit with a few more pages in it. And then yesterday it became clear to me I needed more pages, so last night I decided to submit the whole logbook. So we have got three sort of installments of this document and as we go along, but the first one that I want to you look at is just this one page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have a 126 to help Mr. Ackerman. We are looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 21st of April, DB126. So there is a DB126.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm interested in an entry made on the 26th of June, 1992, which you'll see -- you have the page of it there, and what you're looking at is what's described as the logbook of the 1st Krajina Corps command, and you'll see an entry there that says, "Confirmation of movement of the delegation, Mr. R. Brdjanin, 26 June, 1992." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it says movement of the delegation confirmation, and then in the second column, Mr. Brdjanin, the 26th of June, 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's the same date as this permit that we looked at DB122 just a moment ago, is it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the logbook where this permit has been logged but it doesn't say for how long this permit is valid. It appears to be permanent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now I want you to go -- just a minute. I want you to go now to the date of -- in the logbook, not the logbook, the war diary, to the date of 8 July. It's several pages further along from where you are right now. And if it will help you, I can give you --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You got there, good.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I can find my place, we'll move along here.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Just bear with me a second. All right. If you look -- it's probably near the end of that day's entries. You'll see at 1700 hours Vojo Kupresanin. See if you can find that.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says, "At 1700 hours, Vojo Kupresanin, president of the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina, arrived and discussed with General Talic, the situation on the entire front and problems encountered by our Serbian army. He underlined that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina would do all it could to ensure that our army was organised and integrated as a unified armed force with a unified command and without paramilitary formations." Now, sir, that entry is significantly different from the one with regard to Brdjanin, isn't it? It says that he was the President of the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina, in other words it gives his position, and says that he met with General Talic. It says that he and General Talic discussed the situation on the front and problems encountered by the Serbian army there, that he presumed to speak for the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, saying that the Serbian government of Bosnia and Herzegovina would do all it could to ensure that the army was organised and integrated, as the unified armed force or unified command without paramilitary formations. So that's a pretty extensive entry compared with that of Mr. Brdjanin, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Kupresanin held a command -- went to the command position of General Talic, and the questions discussed were recorded, whereas Mr. Brdjanin went to the operative group and this logbook could not record what was discussed there. This could be found in the diary of the operative group. That is the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, I don't know whether you want to take the time to do this or not, but this logbook where it recorded the permission issued to Mr. Brdjanin, you can search it from now on, and you'll never find that Mr. Kupresanin had to get any kind of a permit or permission, or it doesn't record that he got any kind of permit or permission to visit, which, if that's the case, would indicate that he had significantly higher status than Mr. Brdjanin, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking here about status but from the war diary of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, it can clearly be seen that Kupresanin visited the command post. Now, whether Mr. Kupresanin needed permit or permission or not, I don't know. I doubt he did. But the operative group which Mr. Brdjanin visited is more than 70 kilometres from Banja Luka. There are checkpoints there, and probably this permission was requested and approved because of those checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the war diary, page 173, in the English version, it's the -- the date is 8 August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go down to an entry that begins with, "At 1300 hours a group of people" --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 1600 hours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, you need to look at -- if he has it with ERN numbers, it's 01304664.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the page starts with -- [Microphone not activated]. Am I correct, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1830? Oh, yes, yes, at 1300 hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "At 1300 hours a group of people from Krajina arrived with President Predrag Radic to ask about combat operations and our position on the front. They were satisfied and amazed when they were told how much territory had been liberated and that we all sat down and ate what they had brought." So Mayor Radic from Banja Luka came for a visit, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think when asked about him, the other day, you told us that his interest was only with regard to Banja Luka and not the areas outside Banja Luka. Apparently he was interested well beyond Banja Luka, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town mayor of Banja Luka, Mr. Predrag Radic, is a person of authority. Banja Luka is the largest town in Bosnian Krajina, and in my view, it was logical for him to visit the operative group and units on the front. Therefore, this was quite logical, and why wouldn't such a town mayor visit the units to provide information and to receive information? So that is quite a normal occurrence in communication between the army and the political authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Turn now, please, to the date of 18 August, 1992. Do you have the ERN numbers in that book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, do you know whether he has ERN numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the second paragraph of the entry for 18 August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the number is 4695.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 18th August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Second paragraph there says, does it not [Microphone not activated] "Radic arrived at 1000 hours, to meet General Talic. They inquired about the situation on the front and soldiers from Krajina." Yes?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, that logbook that you were looking at part of a little while ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Your Honours I think it's been marked as DB128, has it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, we have the entire logbook or as much as has been furnished to us as an exhibit, and if I suggest to you that no where in that logbook will you find any reference to passes or permits being issued to Predrag Radic or any group headed by Predrag Radic. Would you accept that or would you like to look at the entire book?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not asking to look through the whole logbook. But as a professional soldier, I repeat, it would be a pleasure for me to be visited both by Radic and Brdjanin and Kupresanin, because this is of great importance for the officer and for the troops, that political leaders should visit the units on the front. How they reached command posts, that is up to an agreement and depends on who has control over the checkpoints along the route, but such visits are normal, expected, and desired.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We are going to a completely different subject now. This must have been your Wednesday testimony, maybe Thursday. It's page 45 of the LiveNote, lines 19 through 21, you were asked about --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that doesn't help, have you got a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I can't do. I just neglected to put the date here. It was at 11.00 in the morning on whatever day it was and you will remember, Ms. Korner, that were you asking about mopping up of the terrain. That's what I'm going to ask about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You gave an answer that asked about that you gave this answer: "The term 'mopping up' implies the clearing of terrain of enemy soldiers, of enemy units. The manpower of enemy units. I'm speaking now in the military sense." And it's correct, is it not, that that's exactly what it means, as a military term, and that you defined it correctly in that answer?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mopping up of the terrain means clearing it of men, in the first place, of enemy soldiers and then also clearing it of the population, which in reality was what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is not what the military term mopping up means, is it? Isn't it true that that term means clearing it of combatants and eliminating the threat to your own units? Doesn't have anything to do with ethnic cleansing, with removing civilians or anything else, does it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It means clearing it of soldiers, soldiers are immediately captured, if there are any. And clearing of the population means moving the population, eliminating them, and that was the aim of those operations. That's what I said, and that's what I meant then, and I'm repeating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when we read in the press reports that U.S. and British forces are involved in mopping up a certain area in Afghanistan, are we to understand that they are ethnically cleansing that area, removing the civilian population or should we understand it in a traditional military sense?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to make a distinction, sir. The goals of the war, the goals in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the war that was waged in Afghanistan. The two cannot be identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But "mopping up" is a term that is used in military circles around the world, isn't it? Not unique to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "term mopping" up or cleaning or clearing can be chemical, biological, because in these areas and in those days, where combat operations were ongoing, we knew what the aim was, and the aim was ethnic cleansing, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go to another issue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, will you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would be a good time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, how many mosques were bombed or destroyed in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 16.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, 1993, don't hold me to the date, and there were 15 to 20 days in between the bombings, when the last one was actually destroyed, I don't actually know. I could have come by that information but I didn't ask for it actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it's the case, if it's true, that the first mosque destroyed in Banja Luka was in 1993, then what you said about forming your resistance group because of the destruction of mosques and other things like that, going on in Banja Luka, could not have been true, could it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not just a question of the mosques. It's also a question of the arrests, unlawful arrests of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, we know there were other issues. I'm only asking you about the mosques. That's the only question I have. I know there were other reasons why you say that you created that group, but one of the reasons you gave was the destruction of mosques. And all I'm asking is: If there were no mosques destroyed in 1992, that wouldn't be one of the reasons, would it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: The resistance movement was not formed because the religious sites were destroyed but for the protection of the Bosnian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please stop. We are going to be here forever if you can't answer my question. And I think it's simple. If there weren't any mosques destroyed in 1992, that couldn't have been a reason for you -- one of the reasons for you forming that resistance movement, could it? That's all I'm asking you. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the resistance movement was not formed to protect the mosques but to protect the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to try one more time. If there weren't any mosques destroyed in 1992, that could not have been a reason or one of the reasons for you forming that resistance movement. It's a simple question. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a yes or no answer. The resistance movement was formed to protect the people and I stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So then what you're saying is that if there were no mosques destroyed in 1992, that it's still possible the movement was formed partly because of the destruction of mosques? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think -- in all honestly it's a slightly unfair question because Mr. Ackerman is saying no mosque in Banja Luka, but what about mosques elsewhere? I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Listen, I'm not here to -- we are not here to answer the questions or to replace the witness in answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now you have hinted at something that probably has given him a hint on how to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, no, I think it's an unfair question because the way is phrased is you're lying if you say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you had a stupid witness, I would understand what you're saying, but you don't have a stupid witness here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, all right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I have to leave that area now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You spoke a lot during your direct testimony about cooperation with local authorities. When you talk about cooperation with local authorities, you're speaking of a couple of things, I think, and correct me if I'm wrong but I think I'm right. You're speaking of maintaining good relations between the army and local authorities and you're speaking of the need to rely on local authorities for supplies, food, construction materials, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know when the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established? Do you know the date at all?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if it was the 1st of March, 1992? Does that refresh your memory at all or do you know if that's a correct date? If you don't know, please say so.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 51 of the LiveNote from Thursday, I believe it was, the 16th, the time signature is 11:36:54. Ms. Korner is asking you about a meeting, she says this: "Can we then please now I think look at a meeting that in fact was on the 4th of June, 1992, at our page 167?" [Realtime transcript read in error "126] And she is referring to your notebook. Now, this is a meeting at the Banja Luka municipal assembly with the President of the Banja Luka municipal assembly and director general of a particular company. You were asked if you'd found it. And then you said you had. And then she said, "And it seems to be dealing with cosmos." Do you know how this meeting came about, why you attended a meeting at the municipal assembly? And you said that you were the commander of the logistics base and the question I wanted to ask you about that was: What is the company Rudi Cajavec or whatever its name is? That was the company involved. What kind of a company is that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Rudi Cajavec company in Banja Luka produced radios, radio stations for the purposes of the army, printed circuits for electrical goods, for -- and it was a very strong military plant, which produced radio stations for armoured vehicles produced by Yugoslavia and other products. I can't enumerate them all. Other goods as well. But it did have production for army purposes, a military production line, and that's why I was invited to attend that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. A different subject now. If you'll recall, there was some conversation in the form of testimony between you and Ms. Korner regarding paramilitary formations fighting along side 1st Krajina Corps units during the fighting in the corridor, and specifically you were referring to the Milanovic Wolves of Vucjak and the formation led by Milan Martic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: First thing, the Wolves of Vucjak were completely subordinated to General Talic and effectively under his command during that entire period, were they not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about that whole period. I didn't have information of that kind. I assumed that that was so, but as I say, I wasn't informed and therefore cannot confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This fighting that was going on in the corridor, certainly there were -- there were Croatian troops from Croatia that were involved in those battles, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume Croatian units from their coast, because the River Sava separated them, so I assume that they were involved to prevent the establishment of the corridor from the -- their military aspects, that would have been quite in order. So I don't know which units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The troops of Milan Martic that were referred to as a paramilitary unit, you were asked if it was unusual or irregular for a political leader, a minister of the government, to have troops, to have a military unit under his command. Do you recall being asked that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the question but not the details, the specifics. However, the corridor itself was vital, not only for Bosnian Krajina but for Banija and Kordun as well, which is where the Serbs lived in Croatia, the Serb people living in Croatia were. Therefore, I see no reason for there not to be units from Krajina there, included into the fighting for the corridor. Not only those forces but others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The specific question you were asked was about whether it was unusual for a minister of the government to be heading a paramilitary unit engaged in this fighting, and I think your answer was yes, that was -- that would be highly unusual. Do you recall that exchange? And if I -- if you don't, and if I'm wrong about it, that's fine, but do you recall it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be logical for a professional soldier to stand at the head of the unit. However, if Mr. Martic was a reserve officer, then I see no reason why he shouldn't command a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that at that point in time, he was the Minister of the Interior of the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was. I think that's what he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know in that position he would have had police units that were under his command, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know that when police units become part of combat units, they become subordinated to the military commanders of those combat units, don't they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That need not be the case. That particular unit can be given a set assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in the videos that we saw, I don't know if you remember this or not but in the videos that we saw the other day, do you recall seeing a video, a closeup, of one of those soldiers who had the patch Milicija Krajina on his shoulder? Do you remember seeing that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that means Krajina police, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That wouldn't be a paramilitary unit. That would be an organised police unit, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony, you at one point, you say, you said that when you saw Brdjanin in 1994, that he was wearing a camouflage uniform. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you were with him at the meeting that you say he attended at Radic's office, what was he wearing then?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me too much. A lot of years have passed but I think he was wearing civilian clothing and that he was not in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You watched videos here in this courtroom of Mr. Brdjanin visiting the front. You remember seeing those?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wasn't wearing any camouflage uniform at that point, was he?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I was looking at the facial expressions, so to be frank -- well, don't ask me about that, because I was looking around to see who else was there and I really can't be sure, so I don't want to answer one way or the other. I was looking at Zupljanin himself and the others on those images. So I really can't say. I think he was wearing uniform -- a uniform but don't hold me to that. I can't say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're talking about when you saw him in 1994? You can't be certain whether he was wearing a uniform or not, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the video, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we make it clear before we move on, is the suggestion that Mr. Brdjanin never wore a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that is the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you concede that you could also be mistaken about whether he was wearing a camouflage uniform when you saw him in 1994?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was at the marketplace. He crossed the street. We said hello to each other, and he asked me whether I needed any assistance. Yes he was wearing camouflage uniform. His car was standing there. He opened the door and then went up to me to say hello, and he was wearing camouflage uniform, yes. I will never forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you describe the car?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a passenger vehicle. I wasn't interested. I didn't even look at the number plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Have you still got the 1st Krajina Corps -- I'm sorry, let me go back. What kind of a passenger vehicle? Do you know what model it was, what colour it was, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in anything like that. I just tried to make the encounter as brief as possible because I didn't want to stay there with him, stand about there, so that some of my fellow citizens could see me with Mr. Brdjanin. So I wasn't interested in the car at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Have you got the war diary there with you still?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war diary, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think it's Exhibit P1590. Just for record purposes, Your Honour. How much time have you been able to spend looking through this document, this war diary?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just here during the trial, in the courtroom. That's when I saw it first. When I arrived. Otherwise I knew of its existence and I wanted to see it. Unfortunately I didn't have occasion to see it before now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you able to look at a copy of it outside the courtroom or is the only time you've seen it is here in the courtroom? It or a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only what exists here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's going to make our job a little harder but we'll do it. This particular version of the war diary, it's called war diary one, extends from 24 June, 1992, to 30 August, 1992, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you can see it on the first page probably.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. Yes, that's how it stands. Yes, the 24th of June, 1992, to the 3rd of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it covers a period --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 30th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- of about two months' duration, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It talks throughout from beginning to end, sir, about battles that were going on, battles that were being fought, in this -- I think the corridor area. There really was a hot war going on in that area, wasn't there, in which people were being killed on both sides?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this document indicates that the forward command of the army at that point was at a place, and I'm trying to find where it first begins with that, if you look at 25 June, 1992, right at the beginning, the forward command it says is located at Duge Njive? If that's how you say that.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, do you go Njiva the 25th of June, 1992, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you give us just sort of an idea about where Duge Njive is located?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never there in the area of Duge Njive. I assume it's close to Prnjavor but please do not hold me to that. I wasn't there. I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the Corps headquarters was at this time in Bosanska Gradiska and the forward command was in Duge Njive, right. And my question is: Where would General Talic have spent his time, in Gradiska or up at the forward command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forward command post was in Stara Gradiska in Croatia, not Bosanska Gradiska, so it's across the Sava River, and the forward command post was in Duge Njive. Talic was at the command post, but with regular touring of the forward command post, which is where his Chief of Staff, Colonel Jelecevic was, Bosko Jelecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So basically would you say that he may go in the daytime to tour the area and in the evenings, though, he would be back at his command post in Stara Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to his plan, and as was needed, he would go to where the fighting was, to see the situation in the units for himself, and that was the duty of each and every commander during wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the things that is reported by a diary of this kind are combat deaths, injuries, persons wounded, things of that nature, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All essential information on a daily basis would have to have been recorded in the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to try to keep this from being too tedious but I want to run through a little bit of this. I want to start, sir, on page -- it's 30 in the English version and the ERN number that I want to you look for is 01304 -- the last four digits are 4531.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 4531, you say. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You'll see at 1503 hours there was a report that three soldiers were killed and more than a dozen wounded. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then if you go a couple of pages further, on the same day, to page 4533.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You'll see six soldiers killed and 12 wounded and two tanks damaged? You see that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now we will go forward quite a ways now to page 65 in the English version, look for number 4563.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you'll see four soldiers killed, 45 wounded, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right before troop morale.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 1400 hours, give me a moment, please -- yes, four were killed and 45 fighters wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go to ERN number 4572, I think, 12 July, I think it's 4571, at the very end of 4571, according to a statement by the commander of the Defence forces.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says 120 wounded, 30 killed, in the Ustasha attack on the town?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go just a couple of pages, 4573, at the very bottom, during the fighting yesterday, they had 31 soldiers killed and about 80 wounded and lists a captain and a lieutenant that were among those killed, Captain Jokic and Lieutenant Misic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, we could go on through this, and if you want to look at each of these, you're absolutely free to do so. 24 July, page 117 in the English version, 8 killed, 15 wounded; 30 July, 12 killed, 11 wounded; 31 July, 6 killed, 61 wounded; 2 August, 8 killed, 31 wounded; 4 August, 5 killed, 23 wounded; 26 August, 10 killed, 92 wounded; 27 August, 15 killed, 76 wounded; 28 August, 13 killed, 26 wounded. And there are more. So a lot of people. There were a lot of casualties, a lot of people being killed and wounded in these fights up there, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And each of these deaths in that period was followed by a funeral in some village somewhere probably in the Bosnian Krajina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, where the killed person had been born, that is where the funeral would take place, if possible. If it was not possible to reach that place, he would be buried on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the wounded, if not capable of engaging in any more combat activities would go back to the places they were from, sometimes absent arms, sometimes absent legs, sometimes seriously deformed, even mentally deformed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The medical corps would take measures to take care of the wounded, and where they would be sent depended on the seriousness of the wound or injury. Certainly, there were many people wounded, and they were taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's talk about another subject now, and this is the subject of morale. Another thing that one notices, if you go carefully through there, is that there are frequent and serious problems with morale among the troops in these units up there fighting in the corridor. And let's visit if we can, just a very few of those and I'll ask you about them. If you look at, it's page 26 in the English version, and the ERN number I'll ask to you look for, you'll have to go back now, is 4527, 29 July -- it's actually 29 June.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You'll see --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's actually June?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you want to look for is ERN 4527. Do you have --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom of that page, then, you should see, "The Ozren battalion refused to organise defence in the Dobrnja sector," and then turn the page over, "completely abandoned their positions and left for Ozren. The reason for this is the poor authority of the battalion commanders, excessive drinking, stealing, and plundering." And then it goes on to talk about that battalion from Prnjavor that we talked about the other day that was looting goods and appliances and tractors and machines and things of that nature. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go now to page -- I think it's ERN 4609.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You see about the Kozara Battalion [Microphone not activated] "...on their own initiative. Some of the soldiers very rude and as a result of that kind of behaviour, five soldiers were killed and 22 wounded and three tanking and one armoured personnel carrier were destroyed." And then if you just turn the page, to 4610, having talked about the enemy breaking through lines and advancing a couple of kilometres, the report along -- the diary says, "This was caused by the Kozara battalion and their cowardice. He wanted to go back to Dubica, the state of morale is very bad, and according to what the TG3 commander said there is a risk of the whole tactical group falling apart because of the bad attitude of soldiers from Dubica and Osinja who are absent all the time and who are deserting their positions." Yes?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 156 English, 4647 is your number, sir. The last entry.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The last portion of the entry there reads as follows: "The units still have problems with soldiers leaving their positions without authorisation and not returning to their positions after resting, which makes the situation at," and that's not translated so I don't know what it says. Do you know what it says right after?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation means firing position, VP is a short for firing position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Makes the situation at firing positions very complex because the first line of defence often remains weakened. The soldiers are quite exhausted and constantly asking for relief so that they can go home. They are particularly angry about looting and other forms of fraud in liberated territory, and there is a possibility of rebellion and relieving of certain municipal officials of their duties." So this indicates that one of the causes for the morale of the soldiers was the looting that was going on about them by some of these other people, and they seem to be especially upset with municipal officials. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what one can infer from the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 176 in the English, from 9 August, it's 4667, sir, which is your number.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first entry, "In the course of fighting today, most units did not even leave their positions to attack as planned. Despite all the measures that have been taken, most units simply do not want to go into battle."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Finally, one more, it's ERN 4672.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just a little ways down after Ustasha's pounded you finally get to morale. "The morale of the troops is quite shaken because of fatigue and because they are still leaving their units in firing position without permission." Now, people are tired and leaving their firing positions and that is effecting the morale, I guess, of those that are staying there and trying to defend a position that has been weakened by the departure of those other people. Is that the way you read that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm finished with those. I want now to go back again to an earlier part of the diary. I want you to look at ERN 4533. It's a paragraph that begins with, "a group of security officers." It's actually 30 June, sir.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The date is incorrectly entered but it says, "A group of security officers arrived from Teslic saying that the situation in Teslic municipality was very chaotic. They said Captain First Class Mirko Slavuljica and Captain First Class Borislav Maksimovic and the entire Teslic brigade command were placed in custody during an inspection investigation. They said that the blame for this should be put on the leaders of Teslic, the President of the Teslic municipal assembly, Nikola Perisic, the chief of the Teslic public security station, Dusan Kuzmanovic and others, and that they had requested assistance from the police in Banja Luka led by a man called Radilovic and arrested our commanding officers and military policemen. After that, a letter was sent to Karadzic to help sort out the situation." Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about that. I was aware of certain problems there but not the details, because I was commander of the logistics base and I didn't know about this. I did know that there were problems there but I was not familiar with the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go a little further over to your page 4536, page 36 in the translation, there is a little more explanation, not much. "The commander of the Teslic battalion, Sergeant Nedjeljko Subotic came and briefly explained the situation in Teslic and the Teslic brigade. According to his statement it was well known who was to blame. The President of the municipal assembly, the chief of the public security station, and a couple of others." And again, I think you probably know nothing about that, I guess?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right after that last entry that we just read from page 4536, sir, there is an entry immediately following that says this: "A representative of the FD of Banja Luka came to visit the command of the Doboj OG." Do you know what a FD is?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. FD? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Go now, please, to page 4539. And it's the first entry. "At 0510 hours, the commander of TG3, Colonel Lisica reported that during a detailed search of the church and the monastery in Plehan which had fallen on 1 July, 1992, nine soldiers were killed and 16 slightly wounded when the building was blown up from a distance of 2 and a half kilometres, although this was expected our soldiers were caught by surprise. The Ustashas were watching all this and 24 hours later, blew the buildings up." Did you know anything about that incident or ever hear about it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about this incident, nor had I heard of it. Plehan is a settlement close to Derventa. It's a Croatian local community. I do know that the church had been blown up, but as to the details, how it happened, when, and the consequences, I was not informed about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just make a suggestion? If Mr. Ackerman wants to read documents, as I do from time to time - he's now doing the same effectively - then it really -- Colonel Selak has been testifying for a long time. I'm perfectly happy for him to read the documents to Your Honours and to me as well, but I'm just wondering whether we need the witness here for it, because at the moment clearly this witness can't assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Read and then put the question. I suppose you do have a question coming up, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the same time, he is also testing the colonel's knowledge of certain facts as they were or were not happening during the last part of his career in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If that's what Your Honour thinks he's doing, then fine by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would never do what Ms. Korner does and just stand here and read documents to you. This is a very legitimate exercise where I want to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sometimes I let Ms. Korner do it, and I'll let you do it. But please do come to the question, especially since we are nearing the time when we have to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to you look at, I think I told you, page 4560. Are you there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you see an entry there about the Sanski Most Battalion? It says, "The Sanski Most Battalion commanded by Major Brajic abandoned its position and is preparing to return home to Sanski Most with booty. The general," I assume that's General Talic, "said that Major Brajic should be immediately sent to prison and tried for failure to carry out orders and for bringing soldiers into a hopeless situation." Do you know anything about that Sanski Most Battalion, and do you know whether in fact, Major Brajic was charged and -- with offences as a result of what the general said?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of the logistics base. These were units of the 5th or rather the 1st Krajina Corps, and at briefings that I attended, these things were not discussed at all. Therefore, this was not a subject of my interest and I don't know anything about these reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I asked about that very entry in chief and he's already given an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you go just a little further down? You'll find an entry that starts with, "At 2035 hours?" It's the bottom of page 4561. Let me see if you can help us here. "At 2035 hours, General Mladic called and I briefly updated him on today's situation on the front." Would you know who "I" is or what -- who the person is that would have -- be responsible for writing this? So that we could know who "I" is that's briefing General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the corps command, there is a command team that is the chief for operative and training activities, and he was a colonel, Marcetic, Dragan, and he was a colonel and that was his duty, and his men. I don't know the name of the person who wrote this, but a war diary had to be kept by them because they had the information. They received reports from units and would urgently intervene on behalf of the commander if an order needed to be issued to the units. The leader of the leading team would change every day but other persons would be permanently there, so this was a position determined by establishment who should hold it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go now to page 4565, and I appreciate that answer, thank you. 4565, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This says, "From the early morning, the Ustasha heavy artillery, especially VBRs and mortars on the left bank of the Sava River has been pounding our positions. In order to neutralise them, our artillery was ordered to attack the Novi Grad area ferry crossing and Donji Svilaj ferry crossings which caused quite a commotion among the Ustasha forces and tanks." This indicates, does it not, that there was artillery fire coming from Croatia across to the corridor area?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that earlier on. An hour ago. That Ustasha forces from the left bank of the Sava River shelled positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, that is shelled the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was it publicly known -- like in Banja Luka, where you were, was it publicly known that this kind of thing that happened -- was happening, that troops and artillery was firing, coming from Croatia, and artillery was firing from Croatia, things of that nature, was that known in the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware of artillery fire, not about soldiers, because my convoys used that corridor to go to Yugoslavia to fetch ammunition, food, and other articles, and there was the question of safety, because there was fuel and other things being transported. So we were warned of the danger of artillery fire coming from the left bank of the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Go, please, to page 4602. It's the last sentence on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "At 1650 hours, we received a report that one Mig 21 was flying over our positions and that all units should be ready to fire on the Ustasha aircraft." Did the Croatian forces have aircraft, combat aircraft?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the Ustasha forces had, whether they had aircraft or not. Personally, I doubt it, because from Zagreb, from the Pleso airport, all aircraft and personnel had been withdrawn to Banja Luka. Among them was a nephew of mine. So that I know for sure that all the aircraft were transferred from Zagreb to Banja Luka, the military airport at Laktasi. But I don't know whether they might have, in the meantime, received planes from someone else. I know of this airport at Pleso near Zagreb, because I saw that air -- those aircraft. I was at the Mahovljani air strip several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you may have heard that aircraft was supplied to Croatia from other sources sometime during the war. Did you or did you not? If you didn't, that's fine, say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I object. What has this got to do with the issues Your Honours have to decide, whether the Croatian air force was supplied with aircraft?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've heard the question, Mr. Ackerman. Do you have an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it has a great deal with to do with it, Your Honour, because what we are talking about what kind of impression that the people in the Bosnian Krajina had about what might happen because of the activities of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What you are suggesting to the witness is supposed to have happened before the period that we are talking about or after?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I truly don't know. He tended to mention it in his answer and I was just asking him what more he knew about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If you have information to that effect, perhaps you may bring it later on, if it has relevance; but for the time being, I think you can spare the witness from having to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really was finished, Your Honour, when Ms. Korner rose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And we need to stop in about three minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll ask one more question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, look at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel, yes, go ahead. You want to tell us something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to say that -- that the airport had Migs 21 and 25, and I personally doubt that the Croatian plane would be overflying this territory which was covered by the airport near Banja Luka. My personal opinion as an officer -- that is my personal opinion as an officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you were of course, in Banja Luka and living in Banja Luka throughout all this period of time, and the next question I want to ask you has to do with that. Look at page 4619, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right near the end of that page, it talks about an invitation that General Talic had gotten to attend an anniversary of 100 days of Banja Luka TV. What -- do you understand that Banja Luka TV had only existed for about a hundred days at that time, that it started broadcasting only in April or May of 1992? Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Banja Luka had its studio before that. Maybe this meant 100 days of the TV studio from the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's it for today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I know how much there is tomorrow now from Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I should certainly be finished by the first break, Your Honour, or maybe earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm very close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we to expect re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour, we've had a witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We also have some questions from this side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of transcript corrections that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in fact there is one which has been -- and which perhaps you can straighten out straight away. I refer to you page 69, line 15. It's when you referred the witness -- I will start the question from the beginning. On page 51 of the LiveNote from Thursday, I believe it was, the 16th, the time signature is 11:36:54, Ms. Korner is asking you about a meeting. She says -- she says this: "Can we then, please, now I think, look at a meeting that in fact was on the 4th of June, 1992, at our page 126" -- it's being suggested to me that that is not the page number that you gave when you were putting the question. I personally think I heard you say a number with four digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It wouldn't be because his notebook is not four digits. Our page 167.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 167, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Now, could Ms. Jevtovic give you the other corrections?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's what was suggested to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because I don't know what they are. She has them written down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm afraid you -- we haven't finished and you have to return here again tomorrow morning. But it seems likely that we would finish by tomorrow. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. If we can first go to page 43, lines 14 and 15? In fact, it's the end of line 15. And the witness gave an answer. He started saying "reej" [phoen] -- And then said "municipal Crisis Staff." The transcript shows when talking about the paramilitary formations, as you can see there. The transcript shows both municipal and regional ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you're saying that he just mentioned municipal ones?

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he did start saying "reej," [phoen] and he hadn't finished, so we can ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. How many of these do you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Just three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just three. Shall we clear them up today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think that's a proper. He obviously -- it can only be cleared up by the witness answering it. I do think this is not a correction of a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if he never said, as it is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is what Ms. Jevtovic says. I don't know one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We definitely have to put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, this is obviously going to take sometime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we can just review the tapes of the hearing. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we don't have time to do that now because our time is over, and I am not going to keep the staff here any further. We can do that tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I agree. I have no problem with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow afternoon, sorry, not tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
